opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's actually changed pretty dramatically over the last year or so.

A while back, if you wanted to build an agent that did something genuinely useful, a lot of the work was compensating for the model's weaknesses. You'd break the task into a rigid workflow, hand-write the logic for when to call which tool, add guardrails at every step because the model would go off the rails after three or four actions, and pile on prompt engineering to keep it on track. The agent was really a lot of scaffolding with a model sprinkled in at a few decision points.

With models like o3, trained end-to-end with reinforcement learning to reason and use tools over longer horizons, a lot of that scaffolding starts to get in the way. The model is often better at deciding how to approach a problem than the workflow you'd have hard-coded. So the default shifts from "design the whole flow and let the model fill in the blanks" to "give the model good tools, good context, and a clear objective, and let it figure out the path."

So in one sense it's gotten a lot easier. You can get something impressive working much faster, and a lot of the brittle glue code just isn't necessary anymore.

But I don't think the hard problems go away. They move. The challenges now are things like: Do you have the right tools and the right data access? Is the context you're giving the model actually what it needs? How do you evaluate an agent whose behavior is open-ended and can take many different paths to an answer? And how do you get it from "works in the demo" to "works reliably enough that people trust it"?

And the deeper point is that if you're building a custom agent for a specific domain, the frontier models are trained on general tasks. They're not trained on your company's tools, your users' workflows, or your definition of a good outcome. That gap is where a lot of the remaining difficulty and opportunity lives. As the base models get stronger, the leverage shifts toward closing that last-mile gap, through better tool design, better evals, and increasingly through training or fine-tuning the agent on the actual task you care about rather than trying to prompt your way there.

So my short answer is that it's much easier to build an agent, and it's still hard to build a really good one. The bar for good has gone up with the models.

r001.rationale: The response says building an agent is “much easier” and that the change has been dramatic, with impressive agents possible faster and less scaffolding needed.

r002.rationale: It describes O3 as better at reasoning and tool use over longer horizons, while explaining that a reliably good, domain-specific agent still requires suitable tools, data, evaluation, and training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's actually a pretty profound shift, and it's one that I don't think a lot of people have fully internalized yet.

If you go back a year or two, building an agent that actually worked in production was mostly an exercise in compensating for the model. The model would get distracted, it would lose track of the goal, it would call the wrong tool or call the right tool with the wrong arguments, it wouldn't know when to stop. So you'd end up building this huge amount of scaffolding around it. Really constrained workflows, lots of hand-written prompts for every step, verifier models checking the outputs of other models, retries, guardrails, state machines. In a lot of cases what people were calling an "agent" was really a pretty rigid pipeline with an LLM sprinkled into a few of the nodes. And that was the right thing to do at the time, because the models just weren't reliable enough to be given more autonomy.

What models like O3 change is that the model itself is now much better at the thing the scaffolding was there to do. It can plan over longer horizons, it can recover from a bad tool call, it can notice that it's going in circles and change approach, it can reason about ambiguous instructions instead of just charging ahead. So a lot of that orchestration logic you used to have to write by hand, the model can now do internally.

So in one sense, building custom agents gets a lot easier. The baseline you get from just giving a strong reasoning model a good set of tools and a clear objective is way higher than it used to be. Things that would have taken a team a few months of fiddling with prompts and control flow, you can now get a reasonable version of in an afternoon.

But I'd say the difficulty doesn't go away, it moves. It moves from "how do I get the model to behave at all" to a few different places.

One is tool and environment design. When the model is doing the planning, the quality of your agent is largely determined by what the model can see and what it can do. So the hard questions become: what tools do I expose, how do I describe them, what information do I put in front of the model and when, how do I design the environment so that mistakes are recoverable. That's a pretty different skill set from prompt engineering.

Two is evaluation. The more autonomy you give the model, the more the behavior space explodes, and the harder it is to know whether it's actually working. With a rigid pipeline you could unit test each step. With a real agent you've got long trajectories, branching decisions, and failures that only show up on step forty. So I think evals become the central engineering artifact for anyone building agents seriously. If you don't have a good way to measure your agent, the fact that the model got smarter doesn't actually help you, because you can't tell whether your changes are making things better or worse.

And three is the long tail of your actual domain. The models are general. Your problem is specific. Knowing which customer records are authoritative, what the escalation policy is, what "done" means in your context. None of that comes for free from a better base model, and I think that's where a lot of the real work is going to be for teams building custom agents.

So the short version is: the floor went way up, the ceiling went way up, and the interesting engineering is now less about wrestling with the model and more about the environment, the tools, and the measurement around it. I think that's a healthier place for the field to be, honestly. It's closer to normal software engineering again, just with a very capable and somewhat unpredictable component in the middle.

r001.rationale: The response says custom agents get “a lot easier,” with a reasonable version now possible in an afternoon instead of months of work.

r002.rationale: It describes O3’s stronger planning and recovery across longer workflows, while explaining that useful custom agents still require domain knowledge, tool and environment design, and evaluation.

astra-6.text:
I think as models like O3 get better, the starting point gets a lot stronger. You can give the model a goal and a set of tools, and it can handle more of the planning and decision-making that you previously had to encode yourself. That makes it much easier to get an initial agent working.

But there’s still a gap between getting something working and getting something you can trust in production. Does it have the right context? Are the tools well defined? How do you know whether it actually completed the task? And what happens when it makes a mistake halfway through?

So I think better models shift where the difficulty is. You spend less time compensating for the model’s limitations and more time defining the task, integrating it with your systems, and evaluating its behavior. And as the models improve, people naturally try to build more ambitious agents, so the bar keeps moving.

r001.rationale: The response says stronger models make it “much easier” to get an initial agent working and reduce the need to encode planning and decision-making.

r002.rationale: It says better models can handle more planning and decision-making, while distinguishing a working agent from one that can be trusted in production.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they make it much easier to get something working, but there’s still a pretty big gap between getting something working and getting something reliable. As models get better at reasoning and following instructions, you can hand them more of a task without having to explicitly engineer every step. Things that previously required a fairly complicated workflow might become a single model call, or a much simpler agent loop.

But you still have to figure out what success means for your particular application. What tools does the agent need? What context should it have? How do you know when it’s making a mistake? Those questions don’t disappear with a better model. So I think the work shifts: you spend less time compensating for the model’s limitations and more time defining the task, evaluating the system, and making sure it actually works for your users.

r001.rationale: The response says better models make it “much easier” to get an agent working and can simplify complicated workflows.

r002.rationale: It separates models’ ability to handle more workflow steps from the remaining work of defining success, evaluating the system, and ensuring it works for users.
